---
title: "Observational and real-world evidence"
subtitle: "Study design on administrative and claims-like data"
---

My training is in designing observational studies where the data was generated by billing, dispensing, dispatch, or death certification rather than by a protocol. The recurring problems are the same across those sources: the exposure window is inferred rather than observed, the comparison group is chosen rather than assigned, and the outcome is recorded by whoever had a reason to record it. I work through those problems explicitly, with a written protocol before the first table, an active comparator where one exists, and a stated list of the assumptions that would have to hold for the estimate to mean what it appears to mean. My dissertation and published work were cohort and cross-sectional analyses of this kind, and my current role is built on linked administrative sources.

## Artifacts

**Mini-protocol: drug-related injury risk on public data.** Two to four pages, structured the way a study protocol is structured. Question, data source, study design, cohort entry and exit, exposure definition, outcome definition, covariates, analysis plan, and pre-specified limitations. [Protocol](../notebooks/rwe-protocol/protocol.qmd)

**Analysis notebook.** A Quarto notebook that runs from the public source file to a Table 1, one adjusted model, and a limitations section. Code visible, no private data, reproducible from the repository. [Notebook](../notebooks/rwe-protocol/analysis.qmd)

**Methods note on confounding and linkage.** Short write-up of how I decide what to adjust for and what a linkage failure does to an effect estimate. [Methods](../methods.qmd)

## What I actually did

- Cohort and cross-sectional analyses of worker health outcomes for a doctoral dissertation and three peer-reviewed papers, from study design through model specification and manuscript.
- Deterministic and probabilistic linkage of prescription drug monitoring, EMS, hospital discharge, and vital records data at a state health department.
- Analysis in R, SAS, STATA, SPSS, and SQL, with reporting in Power BI and Tableau.
- Protocol and analysis plans written before analysis, and limitations sections written to be read by people who will act on the result.

## What I am not claiming

::: {.limits}
I have not worked inside a pharmaceutical sponsor, and I have not run a study on a licensed commercial claims database such as MarketScan, Optum, Komodo, or HealthVerity. I have not built studies in Sentinel, Flatiron, or TriNetX. The public-data protocol on this page is my own work on open data, not a client deliverable. What transfers is study design, cohort construction on messy administrative data, linkage, and analysis, not vendor-specific tooling.
:::
